lesson.title: Carving One Network into Many: The Practice of Subnetting
lesson.summary: Subnetting takes a single large network and deliberately divides it into smaller, self-contained subnets by borrowing host bits for additional network bits, matching address allocation to real organizational structure.
lesson.body:
A subnet, as introduced earlier, is a smaller logical segment carved out of a larger network, and a subnet mask is the tool that marks where the boundary between network and host bits sits. Subnetting is the practical, hands-on process of using that tool: deciding how many host bits to borrow and reassign to the network portion so that one address block becomes several smaller, independently addressable blocks. Organizations subnet for concrete reasons: to separate traffic between departments or buildings, to limit the size of broadcast domains so broadcast traffic does not flood an entire company, to apply different security policies to different segments, and to make efficient use of a limited address allocation instead of placing every device on one flat network.

The mechanics start from a given block and a target number of subnets or hosts per subnet. Suppose an organization is assigned 192.168.10.0/24, the standard 256-address block, and needs to split it into four equally sized subnets. Four subnets require borrowing 2 host bits, because 2 squared equals 4. Borrowing 2 bits moves the prefix from /24 to /26, giving a mask of 255.255.255.192, exactly the mask from the earlier subnet mask example. Each of the four resulting subnets holds 64 addresses, 2 to the 6th power, since 6 host bits remain, with 62 usable per subnet after removing the network and broadcast addresses. The four subnets are 192.168.10.0/26, 192.168.10.64/26, 192.168.10.128/26, and 192.168.10.192/26, each with its own usable range, for example 192.168.10.65 through 192.168.10.126 on the second subnet.

Subnetting does not have to produce equal-sized pieces. Variable-length subnet masking, VLSM, lets an engineer apply different prefix lengths to different pieces of the same original block, so a point-to-point link between two routers that only ever needs 2 usable addresses can be given a tiny /30, 4 total addresses, 2 usable, while a user floor with 100 employees gets a /25, 128 addresses, 126 usable, carved from the same parent block. This flexibility is what makes real-world address plans efficient instead of wasteful; handing every subnet the same fixed size, the way classful addressing once forced networks to do, would burn through address space far faster.

The general formula ties directly back to CIDR notation and the subnet mask concept: for n borrowed bits, you get 2 to the n subnets, and each subnet has 32 minus the original prefix plus n host bits remaining, giving 2 to that power total addresses, minus 2 for usable hosts on any subnet larger than a /31. A /31, with only 1 host bit, is a special case reserved for point-to-point links and uses both addresses without a broadcast address at all.

Getting this arithmetic right, and reasoning correctly about where each subnet's network address, broadcast address, and usable range fall, is one of the most practically important skills in IP network administration, because a miscalculated subnet boundary causes two devices meant to be isolated to instead overlap, or two devices meant to talk directly to instead require a router in between.
